name: Acsah
title: Caleb's Daughter and Othniel's Wife
summary: Acsah was the daughter of the faithful Caleb, who together with Joshua was one of only two among the twelve spies who gave a positive report after exploring the land of Canaan. When Caleb offered his daughter as a reward to whoever captured the city of Kiriath-sepher (Debir), Othniel – son of Kenaz – won her hand through his bravery in battle. Acsah showed both courage and practical wisdom: according to the text, Othniel was encouraged to ask his father for a field, and then Acsah herself approached Caleb directly with a request for springs in addition to the dry Negev land she had received. Caleb generously granted her both the upper and lower springs, a gift of great economic and life-sustaining value. Her initiative and boldness make her one of the most action-oriented female figures in the accounts of the conquest.
roles: A courageous woman in the conquest period

keyEvents.title: Caleb's Promise of Acsah's Hand
keyEvents.description: Caleb promised to give his daughter Acsah to whoever captured Kiriath-sepher (Debir). This was a known method to motivate warriors during the conquest of Canaan.

keyEvents.title: Othniel's Conquest and Marriage to Acsah
keyEvents.description: Othniel, son of Kenaz and relative of Caleb, captured Kiriath-sepher and received Acsah as his wife as a reward for his bravery in battle.

keyEvents.title: Acsah Asks for Water Springs
keyEvents.description: When Acsah arrived at Othniel's home, steps were taken to ask Caleb for a piece of land. Acsah then approached her father directly and requested water springs, since she had been given dry land in the Negev. Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs—a generous gift that secured the family's livelihood in the arid landscape.

versions.summary: Acsah was the daughter of Caleb, one of the twelve spies sent into the land of Canaan. She was given as a wife to Othniel, who captured the city of Kirjath-sepher. Acsah is known for asking her father for a blessing in the form of springs of water, which shows her boldness and faith.

Joshua chapter 15 is correct for this account. However, the parallel reference in Judges (bookId 7) chapter 1 is also correct. No error upon closer inspection.; [minor] The last two keyEvents (Acsah's inheritance in the Negev and Parallel account in the book of Judges) overlap significantly with the third event (Acsah asks for water springs). It is recommended to merge these or remove redundancy to avoid repetition.; [minor] The role 'matriarch' is somewhat imprecise for Acsah, who is primarily known as Caleb's daughter and Othniel's wife. She is not described as a founding figure in the same way as Sarah, Rebekah, or Rachel. A more precise role could be 'daughter of Caleb' or 'wife'.; [minor] The summary states that Caleb was 'one of the twelve spies sent into the land of Canaan.' Although this is correct, it is more precise to emphasize that he was one of two (along with Joshua) who gave a positive report and thus received the promise of entering the land.; [minor] Othniel is described in the Bible as 'son of Kenaz, Caleb's brother,' making him Caleb's nephew (or younger brother, depending on interpretation). It may be helpful to include an explanatory footnote about this family relationship.

footnotes.text: The name Acsah (Hebrew: עַכְסָה, 'Akhsah') probably means 'anklet' or 'ankle band'. The name may reflect an ancient Israelite custom of giving daughters names related to jewelry and adornment.

Kirjath-sepher (also called Debir) means 'city of books' or 'city of writing'. Archaeological excavations have attempted to identify this city. Tell Beit Mirsim in the southern Judean hills has traditionally been proposed, but more recent research also points to Khirbet Rabud as a possible location.

The fact that Acsah herself took the initiative to ask her father for springs of water testifies to remarkable agency in ancient Israelite society. Springs were vital resources in the dry Negev region, and the gift of both upper and lower springs represented a significant economic blessing.

The relationship between Othniel and Caleb is a subject of discussion among interpreters. The Hebrew text can be read as meaning that Othniel was the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother—thus Caleb's nephew. Alternatively, the expression 'Caleb's younger brother' may refer to Othniel himself. Rabbinic tradition has discussed this familial relationship in detail.

The account of Acsah is found in two parallel texts: Josh 15:16–19 and Judg 1:12–15. Such parallel accounts in the Hebrew Bible are often called synoptic texts and provide an opportunity to study how traditions were passed down and written over time.

The Negev region, where Acsah received her land, is a semi-desert landscape in the southern part of what is now Israel. Access to permanent water sources was absolutely crucial for agriculture and settlement in this area, which underscores the great value of Caleb's gift to his daughter.

The Hebrew verb in Josh 15:18 that describes who encouraged whom is textually disputed. The Masoretic Text in Joshua has ותסיתהו ('she urged him'), while the parallel text in Judg 1:14 has the same form. Some textual critics and translations interpret this differently, making it unclear whether it was Acsah or Othniel who took the initiative.
